Turns out that doesn't matter and you can just remove it entirely. > > Anthropic doesn't care if it sees `OpenCode` in the system prompt. Why would they? @jjjermiah 

## Feasibility Analysis: Token Usage Per File

### Current Architecture
The codebase has two distinct token tracking approaches:
1. Actual Token Counts - When messages are processed, providers return real token metrics (input, output, reasoning, cache.read/write)

2. Estimation - A simple character-based estimator (chars / 4) for quick approximations
Key Challenges & Findings

#### Challenge 1: Attribution Problem 
- Token counts are calculated at the message level, not per-file
- When a user reads 3 files and sends one message, the system knows:
  - Total input tokens for that message
  - Which files were read
  - But NOT how many tokens each file contributed to that message
- The read tool output is in the message, but tokens are aggregated at message boundary

#### Challenge 2: Context Complexity 
- Files appear in context multiple ways:
  - Explicitly read by user (via Read tool)
  - Auto-loaded files (via metadata)
  - System context (prompt templates)
- Each contributes differently to token counts

#### Challenge 3: Provider Variance 
- Different providers (Claude, GPT, etc.) may tokenize the same file differently
- Current system doesn't track per-provider token counts

Closing — the original issue was a misdiagnosis. The MCP SDK correctly sets `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` in `send()` (verified by reading SDK source). The real failure was an empty `{env:BRAINTRUST_API_KEY}` causing silent auth errors, not a missing header.

Closing — misdiagnosis. The MCP SDK (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`) correctly sets `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` in `StreamableHTTPClientTransport.send()`. The header is set after merging `requestInit.headers`, so user-provided headers can't override it.

The actual root cause was `{env:BRAINTRUST_API_KEY}` silently resolving to `""` (env var not exported in shell), causing auth failures. Transport failures were logged at `debug` level only, making the real error invisible.
